module_title: Administrative Law & Natural Justice: Foundational Principles
introduction: This foundational level explores the branch of public law that governs the powers and duties of the executive branch. It focuses on how Administrative Law keeps government agencies in check, preventing them from abusing their massive discretionary powers, primarily through the eternal principles of Natural Justice.

core_concepts.title: What is Administrative Law?
core_concepts.description:
It is the law relating to the administration. It determines the organization, powers, and duties of administrative authorities (e.g., Ministries, Municipalities, Tax Boards). 
- Core Objective: To ensure that the Executive (Government) acts within the boundaries of the law and does not trample on the rights of citizens. It acts as the bridge between the 'Rule of Law' and 'Welfare State'.

core_concepts.title: Rule of Law (A.V. Dicey)
core_concepts.description:
The foundation of Administrative Law, popularized by British jurist A.V. Dicey.
- Three Pillars: 
  1. Supremacy of Law (No man can be punished except for a distinct breach of law).
  2. Equality before Law (No man is above the law; the Prime Minister and a peon are judged by the same courts).
  3. Predominance of Legal Spirit (Rights are secured by judicial decisions, not mere constitutional declarations).

core_concepts.title: Principles of Natural Justice (Rules of Fair Play)
core_concepts.description:
Unwritten rules of fairness that EVERY administrative and quasi-judicial body MUST follow before taking any action that affects a citizen's rights.
1. Rule Against Bias (Nemo judex in causa sua): 'No man shall be a judge in his own cause'. The deciding authority must be 100% impartial. (Types of Bias: Personal, Pecuniary/Financial, Subject-matter).
2. Right to Fair Hearing (Audi alteram partem): 'Hear the other side'. Nobody can be penalized or deprived of rights without being given a fair notice and a reasonable opportunity to defend themselves.

core_concepts.title: Separation of Powers (Montesquieu)
core_concepts.description: The doctrine that the three organs of the State (Legislature/Law-making, Executive/Law-enforcing, Judiciary/Law-interpreting) should remain separate to prevent tyranny. In India, there is no absolute separation of powers; there is a system of 'Checks and Balances' (e.g., Judges review Executive acts, Legislature can impeach Judges).

important_entities.name: Pecuniary Bias
important_entities.key_fact: Financial interest completely disqualifies a judge.
important_entities.significance: A deeply tested concept. In administrative law, the slightest 'pecuniary' (financial) interest of a decision-maker in the subject matter automatically vitiates (cancels) their decision, regardless of whether the bias actually influenced the decision or not. There is zero tolerance for financial conflict of interest.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: The 'Statutory Exclusion of Natural Justice' Trap
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners will ask: 'Does Natural Justice apply to every single government action without exception?' **NO**. The principles of Natural Justice can be expressly excluded by a Statute (if the law says no hearing is needed), or impliedly excluded in situations of **extreme emergency** (e.g., bulldozing a crumbling building that is about to fall on a crowd) or academic adjudication (e.g., failing a student in an exam).

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: S E P (Supremacy of Law, Equality before Law, Predominance of Legal Spirit)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use 'SEP' to instantly recall the three distinct pillars of A.V. Dicey's traditional theory.

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a Judiciary question asks 'Which principle of Natural Justice is violated if an examining officer holds shares in the company he is investigating?', select the **Rule Against Bias (Nemo judex in causa sua)**.
